### D-030 — Each realm owns its RBAC merge file under meta/dbTest

> _2026-08-23 · cross-cutting · active_

Commander-specific RBAC (the `commanderAdmin` capability plus the `Admin` role's grant) moved OUT of
`core/blong-access/meta/dbTest/accessAuthorizationMerge.yaml` into the commander realm's own
`meta/dbTest/commander-accessAuthorizationMerge.yaml`; the access file keeps only access-realm RBAC
(testAdmin/Admin, `accessModelAdmin`, `loginCapability`, …). `commanderAdmin` had never been in a
committed version of the access file — it was an uncommitted working-tree addition — so removing it
returned that file to its committed state.

### D-031 — The mongosh liveness probe crash-looped the dev MongoDB pod

> _2026-08-23 · ci · active_

The dev integration MongoDB pod crash-looped even though `mongod` was healthy: the `mongosh` exec
liveness probe (Node 16 startup plus connect) exceeded its 10-second timeout.
`test/integration/mongodb-deployment.yaml` now uses a `tcpSocket` probe on 27017 with a 512Mi memory
limit, and the pod is stable with 0 restarts. It is unrelated to the RBAC work it was found next to,
but it blocked it.

### D-069 — CI metrics deltas compare against the last merged main state

> _2026-09-09 · ci · active_

Baseline storage is option B, a committed file updated by a main-side updater:
`.github/metrics.json` is committed on main and a reusable `update-metrics.yaml` folds the merged
PR's run snapshot into it, so the PR branch is never mutated and no build is re-triggered and no
required check goes stale. A delta therefore means "versus the last merged main state" and the
baseline only advances when a green PR merges. The report renders an aggregate line plus per-package
columns (tests count delta and coverage percentage-point delta); the committed file holds the latest
snapshot as the baseline plus a `history` array of the last ~10 merged runs, newest first. The
schema is metric-agnostic at the aggregate level (v1 covers only tests and coverage), so a future
metric adds a field and a small delta reducer in the same renderer. Everything (parse, baseline
diff, snapshot write, render) lives in the single `render-ci.mjs` embedded in `rush.yaml`'s "Render
CI summary" step, the `metrics.json` snapshot is uploaded as the `metrics` artifact, and the first
run with no baseline renders exactly as before. Keying conventions to keep: top-level
`coverage.lines = {hit, found}` and NOT `{hit, total}` (a renderer bug read `.total` and silently
produced null deltas), and per-package `packages[<name>].coverage = {linesHit, linesTotal}`. blong's
`release.yaml` gained an `update-metrics` job calling the reusable workflow at `@main` with
`RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN`.

### D-070 — Complex CI steps became composite actions in the actions repo

> _2026-09-09 · ci · active_

The shared `rush.yaml` is a REUSABLE workflow consumed with `uses: …@main`, so it runs in the
CALLER's checkout and a plain `run: node scripts/x.mjs` from the actions repo would not resolve.
That had pushed logic into giant bash blocks and heredocs embedded in YAML, which are hard to lint,
test and diff and are full of quoting hazards. The two genuinely complex blocks became composite
actions committed in the actions repo and invoked as
`uses: infitx-org/actions/.github/actions/<name>@main` (GitHub clones the actions repo into
`${{ github.action_path }}` at runtime): `render-ci` (report parse, baseline diff, metrics snapshot,
step summary — dependency-free `.mjs`) and `deploy-report` (gh-pages publish: clone and init, copy,
prune numeric run directories, regenerate index.html, force push, resolve the pages URL).
Conventions that must hold: actions are dependency-free plain node with no `@actions/*` and no build
step; composite steps use `shell: bash` and `run: node "${{ github.action_path }}/index.mjs"`;
inputs flow through an explicit `env: INPUT_*:` mapping; outputs are appended to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`
and declared under the action's `outputs:`; and all filesystem work is anchored to
`$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` by `process.chdir` or `join(workspace, …)`. `publish-report` gained a `- *node`
setup step so Node is guaranteed on PATH. Deferred: the remaining small bash (Assemble comment, List
reports, Config check, List Dockerfiles). Consumers stay pinned to `rush.yaml@main`, so these
actions are exercised only after merging to the actions repo's main.

The repository was reorganised into `core/`, `realm/`, `suite/`, `demo/`, `test/` and `tools/` so
that search and discovery stay focused, with every package at depth 2 (`category/package`) keeping
relative paths such as `../../common/...` identical everywhere. Scope choice: only packages under
`core/` were relocated — `ext/rest-fs`, `docs/blong` and the gitignored `dev/` stayed put, even
though `ext/rest-fs` is dev tooling that would fit `tools/`, because the shared `infitx-org/actions`
CI workflow and both `.vscode/launch.json` files assume `ext/` exists. User-confirmed assignments:
framework to `core/`, reusable realms to `realm/`, reusable suites to `suite/`, demonstration realms
and suites to `demo/`, framework tests to `test/`, dev tooling to `tools/`. Explicitly chosen:
`config-hot-reload` and `blong-kopi` stay in `core/`; `blong-eip` goes to `demo/`;
`blong-access-mock` and `blong-test` to `realm/`; `blong-sim-api` and `blong-sim-tcp` to `test/`;
`blong-ttk` to `tools/`; `blong-allure`, `blong-chain` and `blong-cucumber` stay in `core/`.
Framework test packages merged into the pre-existing top-level `test/` folder (which also holds the
non-package `test/integration/` k8s manifests) and `@feasibleone/test` was renamed `test/framework`
to avoid `test/test/`. `core/common/chromatic.sh` moved to repo-root `common/chromatic.sh`, removing
the undocumented `core/common` sibling trick, and both consumers now use
`../../common/chromatic.sh`. `tools/blong-graph/tsconfig.json` extended `core/blong/tsconfig.json`,
whose `rootDir: "."` TypeScript resolves relative to the BASE config's directory, so `rootDir`
became `core/blong` and every blong-graph source file fell outside it (TS6059) with `outDir`
pointing at `core/blong/dist` — a pre-existing bug, verified with a minimal repro, fixed by an
explicit `rootDir`/`outDir` override in blong-graph's own config, with a note to reconsider a
standalone tsconfig. Deliberately not rewritten: `plans/**` (~1000 stale references),
`.github/memory/*.md` and the regenerated Docusaurus `docs/blong/build/`. `rush.json`'s `projects`
array was rewritten in place and never reordered, because `blong-browser/src/playwright/config.ts`
derives Playwright ports from each package's index.

### D-072 — The blong-theme skill distils the wood variant's lessons

> _2026-09-12 · skills · active_

After the wood variant was accepted the user asked for a skill so future themes are cheaper, "basing
the instructions on the lessons learned, the decisions and frictions during the wood theme
creation". It is workspace-scoped rather than personal — team knowledge that must roam with the repo
— so it lives in `.github/skills/blong-theme/` and is registered in the `[SKILLS_DELEGATOR]` table
of `copilot-instructions.md`, plus a routing sentence in blong-browser's description and body. It is
named `blong-theme` to match the `blong-<domain>` convention, and its subject is specifically VISUAL
VARIANT LAYERS rather than PrimeReact theme families, with components and pages routed to
blong-browser and Storybook to storybook-v10-setup. It has four reference files rather than one long
SKILL.md, for progressive loading: `design-match` (measurement, verification harnesses, environment
limits), `prime-react-cascade` (v10 layer mechanics, focus, CDP), `textures` (tiling law,
calibration, formats, delivery) and `wood-theme` (the worked example with the measured constants),
while SKILL.md stays 171 lines and carries the guardrails, procedure, variant contract and
definition of done. There is deliberately no `scripts/` directory: the measurement recipes live as
commands inside the references, because shipping executable code that was never run would be worse
than the recipes it replaced. The wood caret decision is codified as binding (guardrail 8: stop
after two failed attempts at a pixel-exact detail, get an explicit product decision, and never
"restore" such a decision) — the most expensive lesson of the session and the likeliest to be undone
by a helpful future agent. The stale `wood.css` header, which still claimed that inlining was
deliberate because Storybook does not rewrite relative `url()`, was corrected in passing so the two
headers cannot contradict each other.

### D-138 — The kukum docs keep every link inside the docs tree

> _2026-09-12 · docs · active_

The docs site links only within `docs/blong/docs/`; the first draft linked two files outside the
tree (the package README and the blong-handler skill), and no other doc does that while

### D-156 — Each package's .ci-report directory is the only report contract

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

`<pkg>/.ci-report/` holds `report.json`, machine readable, plus a derived `summary.md`, written by
`blong-dev test` for tap through tap's built-in `json` reporter, by `blong-dev playwright` from
Allure results, and by `blong-dev report vitest`. Nothing outside the repository parses runner
output any more, so a consumer only has to read one JSON shape. The old pipeline reported only the
packages that feed the coverage report, the Playwright suites and `blong-browser`, because each
runner wrote a differently shaped `summary.md` that the workflow scraped with a regex, which made
tap-only packages invisible while the test step streamed every project's full output. Reconsider if
a runner appears whose results cannot be expressed as suites and tests.

### D-157 — Report rendering moved into blong-dev and render-ci was deleted

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

Rendering now lives in `blong-dev ci-report` and the `render-ci` composite action was deleted rather
than left as a second renderer. The workflow fetches the base-branch baseline, calls the
repository's `rush ci-report` hook and publishes what it produced. The workflow still owns the
surfaces — the action summary, the sticky pull-request comment and the published URLs — because
those only exist after publishing. Reconsider if another repository wants the report without blong's
tooling: the renderer would then have to come back as a shared action.

### D-158 — Metrics and history are rebuilt per run instead of appended

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

`.github/metrics.json` and `.github/history.jsonl` are written as "base branch plus exactly this
run", so repeated runs of one pull request are idempotent and every run renders its trends against
`main`. `commit-metrics` pushes them onto the pull-request head with the workflow token, whose
pushes do not re-trigger workflows, guards on fork pull requests and on a `chore(metrics)` head
commit, and never fails the job; merging the pull request carries the entry to `main`, and blong's
post-merge `update-metrics` job was removed. A union merge on the JSONL tolerates concurrent pull
requests, with records keyed by run id and de-duplicated on read, and the Allure slice passed to
`allure awesome` is stripped of our package tag so Allure sees its native format.

### D-159 — The failures bundle is one stable URL built for agents

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

One `deploy-report` entry with `tool=failures` publishes `index.html`, `failures.json`,
`failures.md` and `traces/` for the failing tests only — real Allure results for Playwright and
synthesized ones for tap and vitest, so one report covers every failure — plus a `latest/` alias
that the `report` job removes again on the next green run. `failures.json` is deliberately
self-sufficient, because an agent is pointed at it instead of reading logs or the Allure HTML.

### D-160 — Unused CI steps were deleted and three placeholder jobs were kept

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

Deleted because nothing consumed them: the gist history sync, the `check-report` JUnit step, which
never had a file to read because the test command never produced one, `--verbose` on the test step,
replaced by a `ci-test-verbose` input, the `run-id` input of `deploy-report`, and the legacy
`allure-report` and `vitest-report` globs. Kept as placeholders, as requested: `reports-repository`,
the docker `changes` and `build` jobs, and the `audit` and `deprecation` jobs, which is why blong's
`command-line.json` still declares `ci-audit` and `ci-deprecation`.

### D-161 — Allure's history file is seeded then appended, one record per run

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

Allure's own history file appends one record per run: `AllureLocalHistory` opens the path in `r+`
and appends, and never rewrites existing lines. That is what makes the seed-then-append trick work —
the runner writes the base-branch slice into `<pkg>/.ci-report/history.jsonl` before calling
`allure awesome`, so the file ends up holding main's runs plus this run, and `ci-report` can then
replace that package's lines wholesale without double-counting. Each record carries every test
result of its run, tens of kilobytes, so the committed file is bounded to `DEFAULT_HISTORY_LIMIT` of
20 runs per package: trend charts only look at recent runs and everyone's checkout pays for the
file.

### D-162 — The tap report trusts the exit code, not the failures counter

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

tap's JSON `failures` field counts skipped tests: `core/semantic-log` reports
`failures: 2, skipped: 2` with zero failing cases and still exits 0, reproducible on a two-skip
file. The old guard that never reported green when tap counted failures therefore turned a green
suite red in CI. A synthetic failure is now recorded only when tap exits non-zero and names no
failing test, and the fallback dump of the raw output tail plus "no report that could be parsed"
triggers only when the JSON is unparseable.

### D-163 — Childless tap subtests count as tests, or realm tests vanish

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

The blong runtime nests its realm tests, for example `addGadget`, as subtests that contain no
assertions, so tap records an empty plan (`plan.skipAll` with `ok: true`) while its TAP reporter
still prints `ok N - addGadget` and the JSON carries the subtest's duration. Treating those as "not
a test" silently dropped every realm test from the report: the fixture realm reported 0 total for 11
tests that had run. They count as tests now, and their status stays `passed` because only an
explicit skip or todo marker means a test did not run — tap's own `skipped` counter calls them
skipped, which would have reported thousands of passing realm tests as skipped.

### D-164 — A nested tap run must drop the inherited TAP\_\* environment

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

tap exports its resolved config into the processes it spawns: `TAP_REPORTER`, `TAP_JOBS`, `TAP_CWD`,
`TAP_INCLUDE`, and the child markers `TAP_CHILD_ID` and `TAP_JOB_ID`. `blong-kukum`'s end-to-end
suite runs the fixture realm from inside its own tap process, so the nested tap saw those markers,
decided it was a child of the outer run, and ignored `--reporter=json` entirely — it printed plain
TAP, no report was written, and `TAP_CWD` and `TAP_INCLUDE` pointed at the calling package. `runTap`
now drops every `TAP` and `TAP_*` variable when it detects that it is itself nested, so a nested run
behaves like a standalone one. That is why the kukum end-to-end assertions moved from scraping
`ok N - <name>` out of the console to reading the fixture's structured `.ci-report/report.json`.

### D-165 — Committed metrics and history files are sorted by package key

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

`metrics.json` and `history.jsonl` are both committed and reviewed as diffs, so their order must not
depend on collection order, which is rush folder order; otherwise adding, removing or moving one
package rewrites unrelated lines. `buildMetricsSnapshot` re-inserts the package map in name order
and `rebuildHistory` sorts its records by tag, stably, so a package's own runs keep their order. The
schema is unchanged, so existing baselines keep working.

### D-166 — commit-metrics pushes from a fresh clone of the branch tip

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

Committing in the CI checkout and pushing it means pushing a stale merge commit of the whole
repository, which races with whatever advanced the branch during a long test run — and on a
`release-please--*` branch that is routine, because the bot pushes whenever main moves, so "push
rejected, rebasing once" was the expected outcome. The action now clones the branch tip at depth 1
seconds before pushing, copies the two files, and pushes a fast-forward whose only new content is
those files; the retry path re-fetches the tip, resets and replays once, and reports a notice rather
than a warning. Verified against a local bare repository whose branch moved after the checkout: one
commit, only the two baseline files, unrelated commit preserved.

### D-167 — Hidden report folders need include-hidden-files on upload-artifact

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

`.ci-report` and `.playwright` are hidden folders, and `upload-artifact` drops any file beginning
with a dot, or inside a folder beginning with a dot, unless the `include-hidden-files` input is set.
Every report therefore reached `publish-report` as "report source not found": the local list step
saw the directories on the tests runner, but the artifact carried only `ci-failures` and
`coverage/lcov-report`, the two non-hidden paths, which is why the failures bundle published while
seven package reports did not. `download-artifact` has no hidden-file filter, so extraction was
never the problem.

### D-169 — The legacy theme frictions are dropped as already covered by the theme refs

> _2026-09-15 · cross-cutting · active_

The friction migration drops the whole blong-theme block of the legacy document
(dev/memory-migration/friction.md lines 42-117 and 385-436) instead of transcribing it, because
every finding in it is now written up in .github/skills/blong-theme/references/: wood-theme.md
carries the missing-font limitation and rim ownership, textures.md the -strip/-depth rules, the
over-stretched-octave rule and the payload numbers, design-match.md the decay-profile method, the
multi-layer edge inventory, the clip-offset trap and the browser pixel limits,
prime-react-cascade.md the @layer primereact mechanics, and SKILL.md step 5 the devicePixelRatio
border snapping. Only one sub-detail had no home anywhere, Vite's ?direct query that makes a
page.setContent() harness able to load raw theme CSS, so that alone was migrated. Reconsider if the
theme skill references are ever retired.

### D-170 — One report is rendered once and posted to both places

> _2026-09-15 · ci · active_

The CI report is rendered once, by `blong-dev ci-report`: it is written to `ci-report.md` and, in
addition, appended to the run summary, so the run summary and the sticky pull-request comment are
the same bytes. The workflow no longer assembles a comment (the published-reports table and the
separate failure-link lines are gone); the report derives every published URL instead -
`CI_REPORTS_BASE` plus the workflow slug and run number - which is what lets it be complete before
the publish jobs run. One table now carries result, test counts, test delta, coverage with its own
delta and the report link, so the separate coverage table was dropped. `ci-report.md` is written
unconditionally, never as an alternative to the step summary: it is the artifact the comment is
posted from, and writing it only when no step summary existed left CI with a summary and no
artifact, hence no comment.

### D-172 — The metrics baseline reaches the branch through a stacked pull request

> _2026-09-16 · ci · active_

Committing .github/metrics.json and .github/history.jsonl onto the pull-request head made that
skipped commit the branch tip, so the tip showed checks that never run instead of the checks of the
commit that was actually tested - and on a release-please branch, which the bot rewrites whenever
main moves, the trick of pushing onto it was fragile anyway. commit-metrics now does one thing: it
pushes the two files to a metrics branch named after the head branch and opens a pull request from
there onto the branch under test, kept at exactly one commit ahead by a force-push on every run, so
it rebases itself onto a branch that moved instead of conflicting with it and never accumulates
commits. The head branch keeps its own commits and their real checks, the baseline becomes
reviewable and optional (an unmerged one is simply rebuilt by the next run), and nothing is skipped:
the push and the pull request both use the workflow token, whose events start no run, so the stacked
commit carries no skip-ci marker - a marker there would travel into the head branch through the
merge commit and suppress the run for the merged result. No mode input: the old push-onto-the-branch
behaviour is gone rather than kept as an alternative, so the action has three inputs and rush.yaml
no longer has a metrics-commit-mode input either. That makes the caller responsible for
contents:write plus pull-requests:write and for the repository setting that lets GitHub Actions open
pull requests; with it off the branch is still pushed and the action warns, and the next run
retries. Verified against a bare repository standing in for GitHub plus a stubbed REST API: create,
refresh (PATCH), rebase after the branch moved, and skip when the baseline is already merged. D-158
still holds, except for where the files land; D-171 is superseded, since no commit is made on the
branch at all.

### D-187 — RBAC and ACL docs are three tiers, and refer to the README instead of linking it

> _2026-09-16 · docs · active_

The access-control documentation is split by tier as the blong-docs skill requires: concepts/rbac.md

### D-316 — Trace links are predicted from the reports base URL

> _2026-09-28 · ci · active_

Both reports build the `trace.playwright.dev` URL from the base the workflow resolves
(`CI_REPORTS_BASE`), not from what the publish jobs actually did, so a failed publish still leaves a
dead link behind a report that reads as complete (T-054). The summary report does it at render time
and falls back to the plain `traces/<file>` name when the tool has no published page; `linkTraces`
in `allurePublish` rewrites each staged result at publish time instead. That is why `rush.yaml`
resolves the base URL before `Run Tests` rather than after it - a package renders its own report
while the tests are running, so the value has to be in the environment by then.

### D-317 — The role baseline was regenerated locally, not in CI

> _2026-09-28 · ci · active_

The access user role baseline was regenerated on this machine and committed, because the failure was
a real spec bug - the pivot granted row 0 of a role list that carried no filter, which is the first
seeded role and not `Manager` - and neither run showed a font-rendering difference. A CI capture of

### D-320 — The rebuild is coordinated by two durable counters, not a dirty flag

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · active_

The first cut of the T-174 coordination marked the materialized paths dirty with a boolean row in
core_counter and let a reader fall back to the source views. Review against the production topology
killed both halves. A flag is cleared by any rebuild on its way out, so a rebuild running in process
A that started before process B's merge committed removes B's marker without ever covering B's
edges: B's own drain then sees nothing owed and the edge stays out of the paths until some later
rebuild happens to run — a lost update, which is exactly what T-174 was. The counter pair removes
that: the generation counts every write that skipped its own rebuild and is bumped inside the
writer's transaction, so it can never count an edge that has not committed; a rebuild reads it at
its start and publishes that value as covered at its end, so a write committing during a rebuild
stays uncovered and owes another rebuild. Coverage only grows, and the procedure publishes it
itself, so a caller that rebuilds without going through the coordinator still records what it
covered. The procedure also locks the row it publishes to, which is what serializes rebuilds across
processes — before that, two rebuilds interleaving their DELETE and INSERT over core_path could
collide on its primary key. The reader was reverted to the materialized paths alone, deliberately: a
request may be a millisecond behind a write, but never behind a write no rebuild will ever cover,
and keeping the views on the auth path for a case the counters now prevent would have been the more
expensive way to be less safe.

### D-321 — A management write is atomic with its rebuild; a deferred one is counted

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · active_

The guarantee that the flattened paths cannot miss an update is now split by the kind of writer,
because the two kinds have different things to lose. A write that comes from a request — a UI edit
or an API call — writes its edges and runs the rebuild in ONE transaction, so a crash rolls both
back and there is nothing to rescue: that is why accessModel's syncEdges no longer calls
core.triple.merge with refreshPath false and rebuilds in a later transaction, and why
access.user.remove and access.capability.remove rebuild at the end of the transaction that removed
their edges instead of before it. A write that comes from the seed batch is counted in the durable
generation instead, because one rebuild per merge is exactly what the batch exists to avoid, and the
batch drains until the counters say nothing is owed. On top of both, every process start drains
once: the counters are durable and a rebuild publishes what it covered, so a writer that died before
the rebuild it owed is repaired when the next instance starts, rather than waiting for the next
write. The key that outlives all of it is the direction the paths fail in: a request may read the
paths a millisecond before a write lands, which is acceptable, but a write that committed is never
allowed to be absent from them with nothing recording that it is.

### D-324 — core and blong-access are library realms, and super is how a realm reaches them

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · active_

Every process that calls blong-core carries its own copy of the realm, and the core schema is
created in every database such a process writes to; the same holds for blong-access, which can
supply access control to services that run off their own database. The graph therefore cannot be a
service somewhere else: a solution with two databases has two resource graphs, a resourceId is
meaningful only in the database that minted it, and a call into core is a local call on the caller's
own connection. That is what lets core.resource.ensure be the first statement of a transaction the
caller owns rather than a step that has already committed before it opens, and it is what D-323 got
wrong — it treated the split of business realms as a split of the graph they are all built on. The
way in is prototype-chain delegation, `super.<name>`, because an import would freeze a topology into
the source, a library() function cannot cross realms (lib is assembled per handler group) and the
handler proxy is the IoC path for calls that may be remote or mocked, which a knex transaction
cannot travel through. The requirement that comes with it is ordering: the providing realm must be
attached before the caller, so a suite lists it as an early child (srv, login, core, access), which
the canonical suites already do. blong-party is deliberately not a library realm — it holds business
data that must not be copied per database — and what that means where a party-referencing realm also
carries access is to be worked out.

### D-326 — Delegation reaches an earlier group on the same port, and nothing else

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · active_

The decision to reach a library realm by delegation (D-324) says what a call into core or access
should look like, but not where delegation is available, and the difference is not visible in the
call. It needs three things at once: the provider attached earlier in the suite's children, the
caller in a handler group attached after it, and both on the same port. A realm's whole adapter/db
layer is attached to the single srv.db port, which is what makes one realm's db handler able to
delegate into another's, and it is also why a handler that delegates must be written as an object
literal — a plain function expression has no super to reference, so the function form has to be
restructured before it can delegate. Two callers keep the handler proxy: a handler calling a member
of its own group, because siblings sit in the same local object and never on the prototype chain the
literal inherits, and a handler in another port, which in practice means the test layer, whose
handlers are attached to their own auto-provisioned testDispatch port rather than srv.db. Recording
this closes the question the user raised twice: the remaining 'db/coreResourceEnsure' bindings were
not an oversight of the conversion, they were the two cases delegation cannot serve.

### D-232 — The dev shortcuts run package scripts, and t/p complete the package's test files

> _2026-09-19 · cross-cutting · active_

i/t/p are shell functions in ~/.bash*aliases running 'node --run ci-test|test|playwright -- "$@"' in
whichever package contains the cwd (the nearest package.json upward). Functions, not aliases: bash
expands an alias before it looks up a completion, so an alias's TAB would complete for 'node'.
Completion offers _files_ - the package's `*.test.ts(x)`for t,`_.play.ts`/`_.spec.ts` for p - named
relative to the cwd, since titles would need the runner's own listing on every TAB and '-g'/'--grep'
still work typed by hand. The scripts were seeded so every package that has tests also has 'test'
(17 packages) and 'ci-test' (tools/blong-dev, tools/blong-log); tools/blong-dev invokes 'node
bin/blong-dev.ts' because it cannot resolve its own binary from PATH; core/semantic-log and

> _2026-10-01 · ci · active_

Each leg installs the Chromium revision its own Playwright resolves before it runs:

### D-423 — Configuration collections are maps keyed by an alias, not arrays

> _2026-10-06 · cross-cutting · active_

Stated by the user as a general pattern they are adding to the instructions: a collection in
configuration is a map with a singular name rather than an array, because an array cannot be merged.
Two config sources, a suite and a CR, or two overlays can each add an entry to a map without knowing
the others, while an array makes the order load-bearing and forces whoever merges to concatenate.
The case in hand was the deploy realm portal list, now portal: {web: {...}, admin: {...}} keyed by
an alias that is the portals name: the alias names the generated Service (alias-http), it is what
the errors quote, and it is stable across a profile change in a way a deployment name is not. A
declaration that is genuinely ordered is the exception and has to say why it is: intents is one,
because the trailing intent is what names the rc file the process reads.

### D-428 — The intents split into what runs a realm, what tests it, and what deploys it

> _2026-10-07 · cross-cutting · active_

Deployments therefore stop passing microservice: DEFAULT_SUITE_INTENTS is release, the CRD no longer
defaults the field, and generator.deploymentIntents drops microservice, dev, integration and
playwright from whatever a CR names, keeping release last because the trailing intent is what picks
the rc file the tree mounts. The browser platform has no deployment split, so its runtime layers
(backend, component, action, actions, browser/api, browser/orchestrator) are default-on while its
test layers stay integration-only. A suite's cluster config moved off microservice: the resolver and
in-process self-dispatch are the framework's release defaults, the database adapter's imports and
in-cluster host/port are its own release block, and the credentials stay the suite's.

### D-429 — Intents do not imply each other, but each may imply layers

> _2026-10-07 · cross-cutting · active_

The split that makes it predictable: microservice activates layers for the realms a process already
carries, dev and integration activate the realms their runs need, k8s activates every realm the
suite declares plus those layers so the registry it introspects is complete, and release activates
neither — a deployed process loads the realms and layers its own `--<realm>.<layer>` flags name, soi
each pod carries only what it serves and starts fast. T-265 tracks the remaining work.

### D-318 — The rebuild follows the last write, and a lagging read falls back

> _2026-09-28 · cross-cutting · superseded_

T-174 offered two fixes and both are in place, because they answer different questions. The ordering
half is the real one: the seed phase defers the materialized-path rebuild, and a bare rebuild at the
end of the batch can overtake a merge that entered while the batch was open, so the edge never
reaches the paths — that is the missing blong.flow.find. The runtime now hands every connection a
coordinator (core/blong-gogo/src/adapter/server/pathRefresh.ts), each edge writer registers before
it reads the deferral, the seed's drain waits for the count to reach zero and repeats while a writer
registers during the rebuild, and the last writer out rebuilds what the deferral left owed. The
fallback half is the belt: a merge that skips its rebuild marks the materialization as behind in
core_counter (access_pathRefresh.pending, cleared by the procedure itself), and
access.permission.list augments its answer with core_path's own source views while that marker is
set. The marker is deliberately the durable signal rather than an in-memory flag, because it is
written inside the writer's transaction and is therefore visible exactly when the edges are.

Superseded by `D-320`.

Superseded: a boolean marker cannot survive a rebuild in another process clearing it, so a write
committing during that rebuild was lost rather than owed. The generation and covered counters in
D-320 replace both the marker and the read-side fallback, neither of which is still in the code.

### D-323 — Atomicity stops at the handler boundary, and that boundary is the topology

> _2026-09-29 · cross-cutting · superseded_

The realm add and edit handlers now wrap their own writes in one transaction, but the resource
ensure that creates the entity row cannot be inside it, and the tempting fix — turn
core.resource.ensure into an injected library function the realms import — is the wrong one. A realm
cannot import another realm: in the split topology core and access are separate services, so the
ensure is a remote call by definition and there is no transaction to join, and in the monolith the
same import would make the code behave differently by deployment, which is the property the
framework exists to avoid. What the boundary costs is bounded because the operations on it are
idempotent and self-healing: the ensure returns the existing resource, heals an entity row that is
missing, and the next attempt completes whatever a failure interrupted. That is why the guarantee is
stated as 'the handler's own writes commit together, and the resource it points at is either reused
or created idempotently' rather than 'the whole add is atomic' — the second claim is not available
across a service boundary and pretending otherwise would hide it.

Superseded: the boundary it described came from treating a split of business realms as a split of
the graph they are built on. core is a library realm, so the ensure is a local call and joins the
caller's transaction.

Superseded by `D-324`.

### D-336 — The bank embedding model is the one irreversible choice

> _2026-09-30 · cross-cutting · superseded_

The running Hindsight container predates the embeddings configuration now in
`plans/memory-index/hindsight.sh`, so it used the built-in `local` provider
(`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, 384 dimensions), and the 48 entries ingested while verifying this feature
are embedded with it. Adopting `nomic-embed-text` (768 dimensions) as the plan intends needs the
container recreated from the script, the documents wiped and the backfill re-run, because stored
vectors cannot be re-dimensioned in place. Nothing is lost by wiping: the markdown tree is the
source of truth and `blong-dev memory index --semantic` rebuilds the bank in about a minute. Either
switch the model now or keep the container as it is — but decide before the bank is filled with real
entries, because the cost of changing grows with the tree.

Answered by measurement: with reranking on, local (384), nomic-embed-text (768) and
mxbai-embed-large (1024) rank all 36 benchmark queries identically (92% hit@1, MRR .929, zero rank
differences); with reranking off they differ by noise only (39-44% hit@1, MRR .554-.560). A stronger
embedding model buys nothing observable, so the built-in local model is kept and no wipe or
re-embedding is owed.

Evidence in plans/memory-index/embedding-model-comparison.md, harness and results in
plans/memory-index/eval/.
